title: The ENTIRE History of Britain in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Britain in 10 Minutes
description:
From Stonehenge and Julius Caesar to Churchill and the Blitz, this is the whole story of Britain in about ten minutes: Boudica, Hadrian's Wall, 1066, the Domesday Book, Magna Carta, Henry VIII and his six wives, the Spanish Armada, the Gunpowder Plot, the king who lost his head, the Great Fire, the Great Stink, Queen Victoria, the empire and the shortest war on record. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #britain #britishhistory #england #animatedhistory

beats.say: August 27, 1896. Zanzibar, an island off the coast of East Africa. Britain is about to start a war.
The old sultan had just died, and his cousin Khalid moved into the palace without asking Britain first.
That was a problem, because Britain controlled Zanzibar as a protectorate. Any new sultan needed its approval.
So Harry Rawson, the British admiral in the harbor, sent Khalid a warning.
Leave the palace by nine o'clock tomorrow morning, or we open fire.
They're bluffing. Nobody starts a war before breakfast.
They were not bluffing. At two minutes past nine, five British warships opened fire.
By about nine forty, the palace was on fire, Khalid had escaped, and the war was over.

show.label: The Anglo-Zanzibar War lasted about
show.sub: the shortest war on record (some counts say 45)

beats.say: It wasn't funny for Khalid's side, though. About five hundred people on his side were killed or wounded.
So how did one small, rainy island end up starting wars on the other side of the planet? Let's go back to the beginning.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Britain in 10 Minutes

beats.say: First, the basics. Great Britain is an island with three countries on it: England, Scotland and Wales. Add Northern Ireland and you get the United Kingdom.
People lived here long before anyone wrote things down. Around 3000 BC, they started building Stonehenge.
That's centuries before Egypt's Great Pyramid. And some of its stones were dragged from Wales, about a hundred and fifty miles away.
Then came the Romans. In 55 BC, Julius Caesar, Rome's most famous general, sailed over from what's now France.
Cold, wet, and full of angry Britons. Lovely. I'll be back.
Please don't.
He did come back the next year, then left again. The real conquest started in 43 AD, under Emperor Claudius.
Not every Briton gave in. Around 60 AD, a queen called Boudica led a huge revolt and burned Roman London.
Rome crushed the revolt, and stayed for almost four hundred years, building roads, baths and towns.
In 122 AD, Emperor Hadrian ordered a giant wall across the north of England, from coast to coast.
It ran for seventy-three miles. Its job was to control who crossed from the tribes in the north, in what's now Scotland.
Then, around 410, Rome had problems at home, and Roman rule in Britain ended. The Britons were on their own. Good luck, everyone.
Into the gap sailed new settlers from what's now Germany and Denmark: the Angles, Saxons and Jutes.
The Angles even gave England its name. England means land of the Angles.
Then the Vikings showed up, raiding and settling. Kings like Alfred the Great fought them to a standstill.
By 1066, England's king had died with no children. Three men wanted his crown, and an English earl, Harold, grabbed it first.
King Harold beat the invading king of Norway in the north. Then he raced south to face William, Duke of Normandy, in northern France.
At the Battle of Hastings, Harold was killed and William won. Ever since, he's been William the Conqueror.
William built castles everywhere. Then, twenty years later, he ordered a giant survey of who owned what.
A monk keeping a yearly chronicle grumbled about it. Not one ox nor one cow nor one pig was left out.

show.text: …nor indeed one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.

beats.say: People later nicknamed it the Domesday Book, because, like Judgment Day, there was no arguing with it.
Fast forward to King John. He lost wars in France, then squeezed his nobles for huge taxes to pay for more.
So the barons, England's powerful lords, rebelled and took London.
Seal this, Your Majesty. It says even the king has to follow the law.
Fine. But I want you to know I'm very grumpy about it.
That's Magna Carta, Latin for Great Charter. John didn't mean a word of it. About ten weeks later, the Pope cancelled it.
A civil war followed. But John died in 1216, and his young son's advisers brought the charter back.
Three of its clauses are still law in England today. One says no free man can be jailed without a lawful trial.

show.label: Magna Carta clauses still in force
show.sub: including: no imprisonment without lawful judgment

show.title: Henry VIII Breaks Up With Rome

beats.say: Now meet England's most famous king: Henry the Eighth.
He badly wanted a son to be king after him. His wife, Catherine of Aragon, had a daughter, but no son who survived.
Your Holiness, I'd like my marriage cancelled, please.
No.
Fine. Then I'll start my own church!
And he basically did. In 1534, Parliament made Henry head of a new Church of England. Now he could make his own rules.
He ended up with six wives. British kids still learn a rhyme for them: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived.

show.label: Henry VIII had
show.sub: divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived

beats.say: His daughter Elizabeth the First became one of England's greatest rulers.
In 1588, Spain, the superpower of the day, sent about a hundred and thirty ships to invade. This was the Spanish Armada.
English fireships, empty ships set on fire, broke up the Spanish fleet. Then storms smashed it on the long way home around Scotland.
More than a third of the Armada never made it back to Spain.
Elizabeth died in 1603 with no children. So her cousin James, the king of Scotland, became king of England too.

tag.text: King James I of England (James VI of Scotland)

beats.say: Soon there was a flag that mixed England's cross with Scotland's.
In 1605, angry Catholic plotters hid thirty-six barrels of gunpowder under Parliament to blow James up. Guy Fawkes was caught guarding them.
James's son, Charles the First, believed God had chosen him, so he didn't have to listen to Parliament.
Parliament disagreed, and in 1642, a civil war broke out. Parliament's army won, thanks largely to a tough general named Oliver Cromwell.
In 1649, Charles was put on trial and executed. A king, killed by order of his own Parliament.
For eleven years there was no king, and Cromwell ended up ruling as Lord Protector. Then, in 1660, Charles's son came back as King Charles the Second.
And Cromwell, who'd died two years earlier? They dug him up and put his head on a spike. It stayed up there for more than twenty years.
Then, in 1666, a fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane. It burned down most of the old City of London.
It destroyed over thirteen thousand houses, but only six deaths were officially recorded. Historians think the real number was higher.

show.label: Houses destroyed by the Great Fire

beats.say: And in 1707, England and Scotland officially became one country: Great Britain.
In 1801, Ireland was joined in too, making the United Kingdom, with the flag it still flies today.
Meanwhile, Britain kicked off the Industrial Revolution: giant machines, factories and coal, coal, coal.
In 1825, it opened the world's first public railway to use steam trains.
Then, early one morning in 1837, an eighteen-year-old girl was woken up with huge news.
The king has died. You are now the Queen.
Oh. Right. Then I'd better get dressed.
Queen Victoria ruled for sixty-three years, so long that a whole era is named after her.
But Victorian London had a stinky problem. Its toilets and sewers emptied straight into the River Thames.
In the hot summer of 1858, the smell got so bad that Parliament soaked its curtains in chemicals.
Parliament passed a law in about eighteen days. Then engineer Joseph Bazalgette built London a huge sewer system that's still used today.
Steam power, factories and the world's biggest navy helped Britain build a gigantic empire.
By 1920, it ruled about a quarter of all the land on Earth. Power like that is why, back in 1896, it could start a war in Zanzibar before breakfast.

show.label: In 1920 the British Empire ruled about
show.sub: of all the land on Earth

beats.say: But much of it was taken by force, and most people in it never got a say.
Then came two world wars. In the first, from 1914 to 1918, around a million soldiers from Britain and its empire died.
Twenty-one years later, Britain was at war again, this time with Nazi Germany. By June 1940, France had fallen, and Britain and its empire stood almost alone.
The new prime minister, the leader of the government, was Winston Churchill, a cigar-chomping former soldier and writer.
Sir, the Germans are sending hundreds of planes at us.
Then we'll send up everything we've got.
That summer, Royal Air Force pilots fought off the German air force in the Battle of Britain.
Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.

show.text: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.
show.who: Winston Churchill, House of Commons, 20 August 1940

beats.say: Then came the Blitz. Starting in September 1940, German bombers hit London for fifty-seven nights in a row.
Families slept on the platforms of Underground train stations. One night, about a hundred and seventy-seven thousand people sheltered down there.
Britain held on. With the Soviet Union and the United States, it helped win the war in 1945.
After the war, the empire broke apart, as colony after colony became independent, including India in 1947.
So that's Britain: a rainy island that built Stonehenge, beat the Armada and started the railway age. It ruled a quarter of the world's land, and once fought a war shorter than a lunch break.
Next up: the craziest things Julius Caesar did. See you there.
